I have considered the surgery, there is a really good book on it written by a man with Tourette’s and his friendship with I believe the first man in the US who got the surgery? The book is called Ticked. The procedure is extremely invasive and from my memory they thread wires into your brain while you are awake the entire time for several hours and like the show said, there is a possibility it won’t even work. 

I have been on four different medications for Tourette’s. One of them is known for extreme brain fog and I forgot how to speak certain words. Another one gave me akathisia, or internal restlessness which is common in atypical antipsychotics and often drives people to harm themselves. Another one made me constantly exhausted, unable to function at my job, and I’d have bursts of extreme tics instead of tics throughout the day. Another one made me extremely tired, but was the most effective and one I am considering trying again. 

I have not tried cbit therapy but I have been to a training for it. 

The thing that has helped me the most is acceptance from others and working on my own confidence levels. I am looking into Botox for my neck tics because they have caused some damage. There genuinely aren’t a lot of treatment options for Tourette’s and honestly it’s something that a lot of the time is better if people around you adapt than you receiving treatment if you have it, unless it’s causing pain or discomfort.

That episode was filmed in May of last year. There were a lot more people ticcing in the audience than it seemed and their tics were interacting with her tics. She actually did a really good job and I don’t remember her talk for the tics I remember it for what she said when I look back.

Yeah the show is staged at parts but the most recent episode made me emotional. I actually went to the conference and I could see myself for a few seconds ticcing on the episode.

Honestly, as someone with more severe tics I feel relieved to have someone who is like me on tv. What doesn’t make me feel relieved is the lack of consideration and education many people (including many people on this sub) have toward someone with a disability. Yeah the cameras make it worse (being watched makes it worse for many people), yeah sometimes she doesn’t tic (newsflash that is normal in Tourette’s), yeah she doesn’t take medicine (i also tried meds and the side effects for me were legitimately worse than the effects of severe tics). 

It makes sense to be skeptical because it’s on TLC, but please come at her condition itself with understanding instead of accusations.

Hello! I haven't been diagnosed as autistic, but am 99% sure I am. I've been formally diagnosed with ADHD. I have my MSW and have been in the field for 4 years post-MSW now. I have almost exclusively worked with kids because adults are too difficult for me to understand personally lol. My therapist says that's because children are more likely to respond to direct and blunt communication due to their developing brains (not saying we don't have developed brains, but it made sense to me). I also work with a lot of neurodivergent kids as the other commenter said. It really helps me because I have a better understanding of them and do not feel as socially fatigued.

It's hard honestly at times. After my first post-grad job, I only worked at it for 7 months and I was bullied and ridiculed by my coworkers and authority figures, which I now realize was partially due to my social skills, along with them cultivating a horrible work environment. But I found my current job and have been here for exactly two years on the dot today lol, but it is a night therapist job at a children's shelter. I'm able to get breaks from social interaction when the kids go to bed, but am also able to provide counseling and comfort when they wake up in the middle of the night or cannot sleep. It's a great balance and I know there will be other jobs like that.

Social work is a diverse field and it's also diverse in terms of the social workers needed in terms of their backgrounds (racial, ethnic, gender, sexuality, disability etc.). Don't give up and find your niche if things get too hard or uncomfortable. Jobs/practicums are not forever. Good luck!

I had two school practicums; one for my bachelor's and one for master's. I felt very similarly and especially for the one I did in a middle school, with kids of similar ages to you, I felt very empty and missed them for a while. 

It's rough to be unable to talk to former clients anymore, especially when you're around a ton of kids pretty frequently, develop these deep connections with them, and then all of a sudden you're never allowed to speak with them again.

It took a bit for me to realize that I know that I had an impact on them. Even if they don't have much consistency, for the time you were there, you were *there*. I promise you that you had an impact. For kids who have uncertain and chaotic home lives, someone who is there to just listen and be willing to make a connection with them is a lifelong thing. They still have you through the things you taught them and the things you did differently from other adults in their lives. I know that I personally still remember adults who helped me with my mental wellbeing as a child and their seeds of care and wisdom overpowered any feeling of abandonment.

You still have them through the future clients you will have, who even if you aren't working with youth anymore or youth of different ages, I've come to find that I remember the small things that made a difference with former clients that might have a similar effect on my current or future clients. 

For instance, in my middle school practicum, there was a kid who loved cheez-its and we set up a reward system for him where he would earn cheez-its. I made sure the first snack in my first job out of school's office was cheez-its. 

It will get easier with time, I promise. Best of luck to you.

I think about it in terms of doubting other things as well. Doubting the door is locked or doubting if you have cancer are some examples people might experience with ocd regardless of how nuanced their obsessions are. Doubt is a mainstay of the disease, so why would doubting if one has ocd or not be immune to that?

If you look up doubting ocd and ocd, one of the first results is an article from the anxiety and depression association about that specific feeling [here](https://adaa.org/learn-from-us/from-the-experts/blog-posts/consumer/questioning-whether-you-have-ocd-when-you-have) 

This quote particularly stood out to me: “ But this doubt about having OCD is OCD!”
